title: Elara and the Dragon's Quiet
markdown:
The Grand Imperial Hotel was crimson brick and tall towers. For nine months of the year it was Glendragon Academy. The air smelled of old velvet and magic. Students learned to turn moonlight into jam or speak to stars. The building hummed a song only the gifted admitted they heard, and the rest pretended the radiators were musical.

Elara Meadowsweet’s heart beat like a trapped butterfly. Her rare talent was putting dragons to sleep—hatchlings to the vast ones with teeth like butter knives. Lullabies of moonlight and whispered secrets. The gift made her nervous, especially when the teeth were on display. Being laughed at made her more nervous still, which was inconvenient, because her jokes arrived too honest. She had once told Professor Periwinkle his beard looked like a startled badger. The hall had laughed. Her face had gone strawberry. She had hummed the rest of the lesson into her collar.

Her roommate, Jasper Thorne, performed indifference as if it were a subject he might take for marks. Dark eyes on the middle distance, or on a machine he was quietly taking apart on the windowsill. “Honestly, Elara,” he would sigh, not quite looking, “must you hum so loudly? A worried bee in a teacup, buzzing about bad things.” She suspected he cared. He was simply better at the shrug. He claimed no talent, then fixed the dorm’s flickering lights and knew, to the minute, when the éclairs would leave the kitchen. Elara had watched him time the oven by the way the corridor smelled.

One blustery Tuesday, Professor Periwinkle called the school to the Grand Hall. His beard held more secrets than a lost library; his glasses were never level. The hall, usually busy with floating teacups and griffin-knots, waited. Even the suits of decorative armour seemed to lean in. He cleared his throat like pebbles in a well.

“Esteemed scholars. Something important has been misplaced. The Amulet of Echoing Silences—keeps the hotel’s special atmosphere just so—is gone. Your task, if you accept it, is to find it in the quietest places. Time is short. Though perhaps not as loud as usual, since we are hunting silence.”

Sweat on Elara’s palms. She held her breath and then remembered breathing was allowed. Jasper raised an eyebrow at a stained-glass griffin that had never approved of anyone. Teachers exchanged looks that were not about treasure. Madam Evangeline, Mistress of Enchanted Objects, silver hair in a bun that had never met a stray, gave Elara a nod almost like encouragement—a rare warmth on a serious face. Helene, the flustered groundskeeper, smelled of damp earth and hope and was trying very hard not to whistle a happy tune, which made the tune more obvious.

They set off with a smudged map that changed its mind as they walked, corridors rearranging like a cat getting comfortable. The hotel was a maze of winding halls, ballrooms under dust sheets, rooms that remembered parties and had not been told the parties were over. Elara’s fear came mostly from Elara. Jasper walked as if boredom were a lantern.

The first trouble was not a monster. In the abandoned ballroom, ghost-like dust bunnies giggled and flickered, tangling Elara’s ankles like sprites with opinions.

“I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?” one squeaked.

“A map,” Elara said, because she could not help answering even when the questioner was fluff.

Jasper flicked a wrist. “Go away, fluffy fiends.” A gust—muttered, efficient—scattered them into corners that had missed company. Elara was sure one whispered that her shoelace was undone and her left sock was winning. She tied the lace. Jasper pretended not to wait.

Unusually shiny cobwebs, glowing as if polished by moonlight that had stayed late, led them on. They found a greenhouse gone wild: old vines, forgotten plants reaching for dusty glass, night-blooming jasmine and ginger. Sunlight arrived in pieces on moss. A quiet place, if quiet meant overgrown and slightly spicy.

“The map shows a drop in the magic here,” Jasper said, boredom set down like a tool he did not need. “Something’s wrong.”

Deeper in, past curtains of wet leaves, a whimper. Not an amulet’s clang. Loneliness, thin and uncomfortable. Through moon-pale foliage: a dragon hatchling no bigger than a laundry basket, scales the colour of a stormy sea, silver streaks like lightning. Tiny claws in moss. Snout tucked. Beside it a loose floorboard thump-thump-thumped, a worker’s distant banging parked in the hatchling’s ears.

This was no necklace. This was a creature overwhelmed by a board.

Elara sat. Nervousness could wait in the aisle. “Shh, little one. I’m here. No more worries.” She hummed starlit fields, quiet meadows, the comforting warmth of a hoard that did not need to be counted. The hatchling lifted its head, dark eyes blinking. Whimpers softened to sighs. The talent that put dragons to sleep could also put fear to bed.

Jasper knelt, indifference gone as if it had never been a good costume. His brow did actual work. “The noise. Vibrations from the old service tunnels. The hotel’s pipes. Inefficient.” From his pocket, a carved wooden wedge Elara had never seen him own. “Thought this might be useful.” Pink at the ears, a crack in the usual calm. He set the wedge with the same care he gave to dorm lights. The thump stopped with a click.

The hatchling sighed as if a weight had stood up and left. It snuggled deeper. In a little while it snored, a small rumble against insect-song, the deep sleep of a creature that had been offered quiet and believed it.

Professor Periwinkle and Madam Evangeline stepped from the leaves as if the greenhouse had been a classroom all along. “Excellent work,” said the Headteacher, stroking a beard that seemed to have grown an inch in their absence. “You have retrieved the artefact.”

Elara blinked at the sleeping dragon. “It wasn’t an artefact. It was a dragon. A very unhappy one.”

Madam Evangeline’s rare smile softened the lines around her eyes. “The Amulet of Echoing Silences isn’t something you hold. It’s a state of peace. This young dragon—Flicker—was too sensitive to the hotel’s old machines. His sleep was disturbed. His unease echoed. Small spells went sideways. People felt grumpy and could not say why. We needed a kind ear, and someone clever enough to wedge a board.”

Jasper shrugged, badly. “Simple. Loose floorboard. Mechanical problem.” His eyes, meeting Elara’s, were warmer than the shrug and did not need the rest of the speech Periwinkle looked prepared to give.

They walked back toward the main building. Silas, the grumpy forgotten librarian, a wizened man with glasses on the end of his nose and an ink-stained finger, hobbled from a dark corner. He stopped, winked at Elara, and said in a voice like old paper, “A dragon’s sleep is delicate. More often a lullaby and a well-placed wedge than a dusty book.”

Jasper was already sketching a quieter arrangement of pipes on his palm with a loose quill. He did not frown. He almost smiled, a faint upturn that made Elara’s heart skip. Somewhere behind the glass, Flicker snored, and the hotel’s atmosphere, for the first time that Tuesday, sat just so.
characters: Elara Meadowsweet (nervous pupil with a gift for persuading dragons to nap), Jasper Thorne (a dorm mate who pretends not to care)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic mystery adventure for older children
